title: Sandakphu Packing List and Altitude Safety
meta_description: What to pack for the Sandakphu trek by season, how to avoid altitude sickness at 3,636 m, cold, water, signal and power, and what to do if someone falls ill.
summary: Pack light, about 7–9 kg, because lodges give you bedding and meals: layers, a down jacket, a rain shell, good boots, a filter bottle, a headtorch and cash. Sandakphu, at 3,636 m, is high enough for altitude sickness, so climb gradually, drink water, skip alcohol and descend if symptoms grow worse.

sections.heading: The short answer
paras: The Sandakphu trek is a lodge trek, so you do not carry a tent, stove or food for days. You carry clothing for cold mornings and windy afternoons, rain gear, a few essentials and cash. A pack of 7–9 kg for a walker, or a small duffel for a Land Rover trip, is plenty. Anything more and you will curse it on the climb to Chitrey.

The two things that catch trekkers out are cold and altitude. Nights at Sandakphu fall below freezing from late October to March, and lodges are unheated apart from the dining room stove. And the ridge rises from about 2,150 m at Maneybhanjan to 3,636 m at Sandakphu, high enough for acute mountain sickness, especially for anyone who arrives quickly by Land Rover. Both are easy to manage with the right kit and a sensible pace.
Gear for hire is limited at Maneybhanjan, so buy or rent anything missing in Darjeeling, where a few trekking shops near the Mall and Chowk Bazaar hire down jackets and sleeping bags.

sections.heading: What to pack
paras: This is the list we use for an autumn trek. In spring, swap the heavy down jacket for a lighter one and add a second rain layer; in winter, add the extras in the next section.

sections.heading: Packing light, and what to leave behind
paras: Walkers usually carry their own day pack and either carry the rest or hand a duffel to a porter. Land Rover travellers can bring more, but space in the back is tight and bags ride on the roof in dust and sometimes rain, so pack everything in a waterproof liner or strong plastic bags.

Leave jeans, cotton sweatshirts, hair dryers, heavy books and spare shoes in Darjeeling; most hotels and hostels there will store a bag for a few days, often free or for a small fee. Leave behind too much electronics: a phone, a power bank and perhaps a camera is enough when charging is paid and limited.
list: A small first-aid kit: painkillers, blister plasters, oral rehydration salts, antiseptic, a crepe bandage and any personal medicines.
Toilet paper, hand sanitiser and a small towel; lodge toilets are basic and water is cold.
Snacks from Darjeeling: dry fruit, nuts, chocolate and glucose biscuits for the long stretches.
Earplugs, because lodge walls are thin and dining rooms are noisy until late on busy October nights.
A small rubbish bag to carry your wrappers and batteries back down.

sections.heading: Extras for winter and spring
paras: From December to February, nights at Sandakphu fall to −5 to −10 °C and snow is common above Tonglu. Add a four-season sleeping bag or a warm bag to use under the lodge quilts, a down jacket rated for well below freezing, thick socks, a balaclava or buff, waterproof gloves and microspikes for icy stretches of track. Gaiters help in fresh snow. Ask in Maneybhanjan whether upper lodges are open and the Land Rover track is passable, since snow closes both; check current status before you travel.

In April and May, carry a poncho or pack cover as well as a rain jacket, because afternoon thunderstorms are common. Leeches can appear on the lower forest stretches in wet weather, especially in late May and late September; salt or a leech sock helps, and they are harmless, just unpleasant.

sections.heading: Altitude: how high is too high
paras: Acute mountain sickness can start above about 2,500 m, and Sandakphu sits at 3,636 m. On foot, the ridge is a gradual climb: you sleep at about 2,970 m at Tumling, 3,186 m at Kalipokhri and 3,636 m at Sandakphu, gaining a few hundred metres of sleeping height each night. That is close to the gentle profile doctors recommend, and most walkers feel only a mild headache or poor sleep, if anything.

By Land Rover, you gain about 1,500 m in one morning. That is where problems come from. Headache, nausea, tiredness, loss of appetite and broken sleep on the first night at Sandakphu are common among riders, and occasionally symptoms become serious. Older travellers, small children and anyone with heart or lung problems should take extra care and consult a doctor before going.

Children deserve a special word. They often cannot describe a headache or nausea clearly, and may simply become quiet, cranky or refuse food. Watch them closely on the first night at Kalipokhri or Sandakphu, keep them warm and fed, and be ready to descend if they seem unwell. Walking up, rather than riding, is far kinder to young bodies.
list: Sleep at least one night in Darjeeling, at about 2,050 m, before the trek.
Walk slowly enough to talk, especially on the climbs to Chitrey, Kalipokhri and Sandakphu.
Drink 3–4 litres of water a day; the cold dulls thirst.
Avoid alcohol and sleeping pills until you are back below 2,500 m.
Consider splitting day two at Gairibas if anyone is struggling.
Ask your doctor about acetazolamide before the trip if you are going up by Land Rover or have had altitude trouble before.

sections.heading: When to turn back
paras: Mild symptoms that ease with rest, water and a night's sleep are normal. Warning signs are different, and the rule in the mountains is simple: if symptoms get worse, go down, even at night. A descent of 400–500 m usually brings rapid relief.

Tell your guide at once if anyone has a severe headache that painkillers do not ease, repeated vomiting, unusual breathlessness at rest, a wet cough, confusion, slurred speech or difficulty walking in a straight line. These can be signs of high-altitude cerebral or pulmonary oedema, which can be fatal. From Sandakphu, the fastest way down is a Land Rover toward Maneybhanjan or on foot toward Srikhola. Medical help on the ridge is very limited; the nearest proper hospital is in Darjeeling. Travel insurance that covers trekking to 4,000 m is worth having.

sections.heading: Phones, power and practical safety
paras: Mobile signal on the ridge is patchy. Indian networks work in places, Nepali networks in others, and some stretches have none. Tell family you may be out of touch for a day or two at a time. Lodges run on solar power or limited supply and many charge ₹50–150 to charge a phone or power bank, so carry a full power bank and keep phones warm at night, since batteries drain fast in the cold.

Stay with your guide in mist; the trail crosses the border several times and side paths lead into Nepal. Carry photo ID for SSB and Nepal police checks at Tumling, Jaubari and Kalipokhri: Indians a passport or voter ID, foreigners a passport with a valid Indian visa. The ID rules at border posts and the guide mandate change, so check current status before you travel.

Finally, carry out what you carry in. Lodges burn or bury rubbish, and plastic bottles, wrappers and batteries have nowhere to go on a ridge with no road services. A small rubbish bag in your pack, emptied in Darjeeling, keeps the trail clean.

faqs.q: What should I pack for the Sandakphu trek?
faqs.a: A down jacket, two thermal base layers, a fleece, a rain jacket, trekking trousers, broken-in boots, a warm hat and gloves, a sleeping bag liner, a headtorch, a filter bottle, sunscreen, sunglasses, trekking poles, a power bank, photo ID and enough cash for the whole trek. Lodges provide quilts and meals, so aim for a 7–9 kg pack.

faqs.q: Do I need a sleeping bag for Sandakphu?
faqs.a: Not usually from March to November, because lodges and trekkers' huts provide heavy quilts. A sleeping bag liner keeps you clean and adds warmth. From December to February, when nights fall to −5 to −10 °C, carry a warm sleeping bag to use under the quilts, especially at Sandakphu and Phalut.

faqs.q: Can I get altitude sickness at Sandakphu?
faqs.a: Yes. Sandakphu is 3,636 m, high enough for acute mountain sickness, especially if you arrive quickly by Land Rover, which gains about 1,500 m in a morning. Walkers who climb over three days rarely have more than a mild headache. Sleep in Darjeeling first, drink water, avoid alcohol and descend if symptoms worsen.

faqs.q: What are the warning signs of serious altitude sickness?
faqs.a: A severe headache that painkillers do not ease, repeated vomiting, breathlessness at rest, a wet cough, confusion, slurred speech or trouble walking straight. These can signal cerebral or pulmonary oedema and need immediate descent. From Sandakphu, go down by Land Rover toward Maneybhanjan or on foot toward Srikhola, and seek medical care in Darjeeling.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network on the Sandakphu trek?
faqs.a: Patchy. Indian networks such as Jio and Airtel work in places, Nepali networks in others, and some stretches have no signal at all. Expect to be out of touch for a day or more at a time. Tell family in advance, keep your guide's number saved and carry a charged power bank.

faqs.q: Can I charge my phone on the Sandakphu trek?
faqs.a: Usually yes, but power is limited. Many lodges run on solar panels or restricted supply and charge ₹50–150 to charge a phone or power bank, and power may be off by late evening. Carry a 10,000–20,000 mAh power bank, keep devices warm at night, and switch on flight mode where there is no signal.

faqs.q: What shoes are best for the Sandakphu trek?
faqs.a: Broken-in trekking boots with good grip and ankle support. The trail is stony and steep in places, the descents to Srikhola and Gorkhey are hard on ankles, and mornings can be wet or icy. Sports shoes manage in dry autumn weather on the climb, but boots are better. Never start the trek in new boots.

faqs.q: Do I need microspikes for Sandakphu?
faqs.a: Only in winter. From late December to February, snow and ice can cover the track above Tonglu, and microspikes make walking much safer. In autumn and spring they are not needed. Ask at Maneybhanjan about conditions before setting out, since snow can also close lodges and the Land Rover track; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there a hospital on the Sandakphu trek?
faqs.a: No. There is no hospital on the ridge, and medical help is very limited. The nearest proper hospital is in Darjeeling, several hours away. Carry a basic first-aid kit with painkillers, blister plasters, oral rehydration salts and any personal medicines, and buy travel insurance that covers trekking up to about 4,000 m.
